Glasgow-1024.public_addition_wikitext:
=== Possible James Glasco of Omagh ===
The 1786 marriage column names James Glasco, Omagh publican aged 61, and Jane Murray of the same place aged 16.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050075355/ The Public Register, or, Freeman's Journal, 1786-09-05, p.3].</ref>

Three 1793 Hope advertisements name James Glasco, Omagh, as a freight/passage contact; the 25 May issue adds a sailing delay.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021067/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-11, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021086/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-18, p.4].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021100/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-25, p.1].</ref>

The marriage was reported by 5 September 1786; the exact ceremony day is not given. James’s reported age suggests birth about 1724–1725. The same uncommon name and Omagh business context support, without proving, continuity with the 1793 contact. The notices do not name his parents or establish a previous marriage.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated birth c.1722 and Moneymore context are compatible; neither identifies the Omagh publican.

=== Possible James Glascow, Fogs Manor postal addressee ===
James Glascow, Fogs Manor, is listed among letters remaining in the Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39395391/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1757-04-07, p.1].</ref>

Fogs Manor is the printed address qualifier. A neighbouring "Phil. Co." in a separate alphabetic column is not this man’s address. The list states no occupation, so it does not identify him as the later Greenwich Packet master.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated c.1722 birth is chronologically plausible; death date absent. Irish location is not a concrete contradiction. The postal record states no occupation.

=== Possible James Glascow, master of Greenwich Packet ===
Greenwich Packet: James Glascow, master; James Young, owner; from Philadelphia to Winyew, Carolina; with rum, bread, flour and porter.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/34421452/ The Public Advertiser, 1777-05-14, p.2].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/396765804/ The Ipswich Journal, 1777-05-17, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971522063/ The Gloucester Journal, 1777-05-19, p.1].</ref>

James Young is the separate vessel owner, not another form of the master’s name. Three issues repeat one voyage report. Neither the route nor the cargo establishes the master’s family or identifies him with the 1757 Fogs Manor addressee.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated c.1722 birth is chronologically plausible; death date absent. Irish location is not a concrete contradiction.

=== Possible James Glasgow, Edinburgh game certificate, 1789 ===
James Glasgow, Esq., Edinburgh, appears in the Mid-Lothian game-duty list of certificates issued since 8 September 1789.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/601822968/ The Edinburgh Advertiser, 1789-12-11, p.8].</ref>

The list gives an Edinburgh designation but no age or relatives; it is not evidence of a military or maritime career.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Birth c.1722, estimated, County Londonderry; death date not recorded. Chronologically possible, but no Edinburgh/certificate connection is documented.

An 1845 tenant-right discussion quotes Samuel Glasgow, described as an intelligent farmer examined at Moneymore, advocating secure tenure and protection against rent charged on improvements. He described seeing reclamation on Sir Thomas Staples’s land in his neighbourhood.<ref>Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 19 March 1845, p. 1, Ulster tenant-right discussion; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050103241/ record]; Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 19 March 1845, p. 1, alternate archive image of tenant-right passage; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1380777866/ record].</ref> Moneymore is where he was examined, not an explicit home townland. The date of his examination, age and relatives are unstated. Cookstown farmers [[Glasgow-2054]] and [[Glasgow-1698]] are compatible; [[Glasgow-2908|Lisnagaver Glasgow]] is a weaker regional comparison, without a locality or occupation bridge. No connection to Lisnagaver is established. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow of Broughshane appears in the Royal Belfast Academical Institution school prizes in June 1830 and Belfast College examinations reported in May 1831. The 1831 report also names James Glasgow, Institution, in voluntary advanced mathematical examinations.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 29 June 1830, p.3, Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390569859/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 6 May 1831, p.3, Belfast College report dated 30 April; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545285/ record].</ref> [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] and James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] are strong compatible candidates. The newspaper gives no ages or parents and does not call these men brothers. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow resigned as an assistant in the Royal Belfast Institution’s Mathematical and Mercantile School in December 1836. Rev. Adam D. Glasgow received a unanimous call to Berry Street Presbyterian Church, Belfast, in January 1840 and was its newly ordained minister at a congregational presentation on 5 March.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 10 January 1837, p.2, resignation presentation on 22 December 1836; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390542489/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 17 January 1840, p.2, Berry Street ministerial call; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390553900/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 10 March 1840, p.2, Berry Street soiree on 5 March; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390555182/ record].</ref> The repeated name and institutional setting support the education/teaching continuity; the ministerial continuation and attribution to [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] remain qualified. The newspaper does not spell out Dickie or identify parents. 5 March is the presentation date, not a proved ordination date. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A marriage notice reports that on 30 December 1841 Rev. Adam Glasgow married Miss Jane Thompson at the house of her uncle, Thomas Corbett, Esq., on May-street. The date 30 December is derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January issue.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 4 January 1842, p. 3, marriage notice for Rev. Adam Glasgow and Miss Jane Thompson; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552100/ record].</ref> The notice records Rev. Adam Glasgow as groom and Miss Jane Thompson as bride, married on 30 December 1841 (derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January 1842 issue). Thomas Corbett is described as the bride’s uncle; no parentage or family branch is stated. May-street identifies the house where the notice says the wedding took place, not Adam’s residence. This is compatible with, but does not prove, identification of the bride as the tree-linked Jane Fulton (Thompson) Glasgow or the groom as [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A designation report names the Rev. Adam Glasgow among four ministers set apart as missionaries to India and explicitly says he was “brother of the Rev. Jas. Glasgow.”<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 January 1842, p. 2, designation of four missionaries to India; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552341/ record].</ref> The report explicitly describes the named Rev. Adam Glasgow as brother of Rev. Jas. Glasgow. This is a report of the same missionary-designation service also reported by the Freeman’s Journal on 14 January 1842; independence between reports is not assumed. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. An India Mission prayer-meeting notice reports that letters from Rev. Adam Glasgow and Rev. Mr. Spier were read at Rosemary-street Church.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 28 March 1843, p. 2, India Mission prayer meeting and letters; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560193/ record].</ref> The notice names Rev. Adam Glasgow as a letter author in the India Mission context. It gives no middle name, home locality, or unique identity bridge. The Belfast church is the meeting venue, not a stated residence or congregation for Adam. This is consistent with, but does not uniquely identify, [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A report of the 10 March 1841 meeting at Rev. Dr. Hanna’s Rosemary-street Church names Rev. Adam Glasgow among the clergy “on and around the platform.” Malone follows Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie, not Adam.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 March 1841, p. 3, clergy and deputation meeting/platform report; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390556571/ record].</ref> This report identifies Rev. Adam Glasgow among clergy at the meeting; it does not state his residence or uniquely identify him as [[Glasgow-1781]]. Malone belongs to Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. At the Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree on 18 August 1840, devotional exercises were conducted by “the Rev. Adam Glasgow, of Berry-street.” “Of Berry-street” is his printed church association, not proof of residence.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 21 August 1840, p. 2, Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560975/ record].</ref> “Of Berry-street” is the printed church association for Rev. Adam Glasgow, not proof of residence. A separate later passage names Rev. James Glasgow, Missionary to India; this is compatible with [[Glasgow-1780]] but does not uniquely identify him. Their co-occurrence is not evidence of kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Marriage notice: on 25 July 1840 (reported as “25th ult.”), Mr James Small, of Lottery Cottage, county Armagh, married Miss Margaret Small of this town; the officiant was Rev. Adam Glasgow.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 7 August 1840, p. 3; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560450/ record].</ref> Minister/officiant occurrence, not kinship. Keep adjacent London/St George’s wedding separate. Strongly compatible with [[Glasgow-1781]], without unique identification. The identification remains uncertain.

Separate soirée passage: at a Tuesday-evening meeting on 27 October at the New School-house connected with the Presbyterian Church, Townsend-street, Rev. Adam Glasgow opened the proceedings; Rev. Josias Wilson closed with prayer.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 30 October 1840, p. 2; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563103/ record].</ref> Keep both distinct passages in one page row and one clip asset, with Adam as an additional excerpt. Strongly compatible with [[Glasgow-1781]]; no kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

Strongly compatible with [[Glasgow-1781]]; no kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

General Synod report separately says ordained Ministers Messrs Adam Glasgow and James Carr offered themselves for foreign mission in India and were accepted; initial field Kathiawar/Guzerat, planned departure 4 August overland to Bombay.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 July 1840, p. 1; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390559244/ record].</ref> This is James Carr, not James Glasgow in adjacent set-apart report. Planned departure is not proof journey occurred. The identification remains uncertain.

Glasgow-1549.remote_wikitext: == Biography == John Glasgow was the progenitor of the Glasgow family in Blair, Cambria, Clearfield and Huntingdon Counties of Central Pennsylvania. John Glasgow (who is being designated as John Glasgow the 1st) and his wife Margaret Hunter were prominent citizens of Glasgow, Scotland. They and their two young sons Richard and John(2) sailed for America in 1781. The exact year when John Glasgow and his wife came to America was established when Margaret had a son, William, on the voyage over. In the Census records the place of birth for William Glasgow is shown as the Ocean, or the Atlantic Ocean and the year of birth as 1781. It is not known what ship they sailed or specifically what the reason was for their leaving their homeland. One account has them sailing from Ireland and landing in Delaware. This could be accurate as in the late 1600s, England had sent groups of Scotch to Ireland to defend the various interests of England. The Scotch established themselves in Ireland, then England deliberately crushed Irish commerce and industries by enacting laws prohibiting the export of cattle, milk, butter, cheese, and later woolens. The English treatment of Ireland had tow results as far as immigration: (1) the economy of Ireland gradually declined which resulted in lower standard of living and (2) among the Scotch-Irish, dislike of the English grew. THe American Revolution received much sympathy in the Presbyterians who were prohibited from holding office. Most Scots were Presbyterians. Consider the economic climate in Ireland compared to what the Scotch in Ireland perceived the climate to be in America. In the New Country there was untold quantities of land available, just for moving onto it and improving it; wild game in large quantities, with no prohibition on shooting it; timber and firewood is unlimited amounts (lumber was scarce in Ireland). It is not wonder that the people immigrated to America where life certainly was difficult and harsh but no more so than they had been used to in Ireland; and they had much more control of their destiny here. It is hard for us to imagine what life was like for the early immigrants as they arrived and settled in this area. We have no detailed record of the Glasgows early experiences in this country. == Sources == * https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/details/G7MK-866 * Will of John Glasgow. "Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994," images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L99B-T8NH?cc=1999196&wc=9PM6-7MN%3A268496101%2C268530601 : 3 July 2014), Huntingdon > Wills 1822-1847 vol 3-4 > image 103 of 607; county courthouses, Pennsylvania.

== Biography ==
7 February 1527/28: Thomas Gleschow is listed with Quothquan tenants fined for nonappearance in a case concerning breach of the lord’s judicial prohibition (called his “fence” in the text). The heading says 1527; Dickinson’s Appendix B assigns the court to 1527/28.<ref>William Croft Dickinson (ed.), Court Book of the Barony of Carnwath 1523–1542 (1937), printed pp.64–65, index p.217; Appendix B p.cxx; PDF 193–194; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=193. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

The remaining Thomas passages belong to five court meetings in all: 7 and 23 February 1527/28, 10 March 1527/28, 27 March 1528 and 20 May 1528. The February and 10 March meetings are entered twice. At the 27 March court Thomas is included in the tenant group adjudged to have broken two judicial prohibitions: cultivating Newmains while restricted and paying rents out despite an arrestment. Fines and imprisonment for a year at the lord’s will were decreed; actual imprisonment is not established. These proceedings name no Glasgow relative.<ref>Dickinson (1937), printed pp.64–70,79–88; Appendix B p.cxx; PDF193–199,208–217,125; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=214. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The tenant list begins “in Quodquen” on p.64; Thomas Gleschow falls before the separate Carswell names on p.65. This supports Quothquan itself, not merely the broad barony. John and Thomas form a plausible local family group, with their degree of kinship unknown. [[Glasgow-1095|John Glasgow]] is the leading possible existing-profile comparison for the Quothquan John, not a proved identification or parent of Thomas.



The five meetings are treated as one tenant’s career. The rolls do not identify his exact individual holding or establish that he inherited from John. Leases and tenancy succession might identify kin. No compatible existing profile was found in the bounded duplicate audit; the Dublin 1725 and Calton 1886 Thomas accounts have incompatible chronologies.

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

Sarah Glasgow was a daughter of [[Glasgow-428|William Glasgow]] of Currituck, North Carolina. Her father named her in his will of 30 September 1746, proved 7 April 1747.<ref name="William1746">[https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/wills/glasgowwilliam1746.html William Glasgow will, 30 September 1746; proved 7 April 1747, North Carolina State Archives MARS 12.96.1.805; NCGenWeb published transcription checked 17 October 2026].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Her mother, exact dates and later identity remain unknown. The will names her paternal siblings Caleb, Abiah and Elizabeth; the identification of the adult Caleb profiles remains probable. The unnamed grandfather and the wife’s unborn child are not assigned modern identities. The contingent land interest and cattle in a mark given by an unnamed grandfather belong to Sarah’s bequest; the will does not name that grandfather. The account is based on the checked published transcription; the manuscript has not been newly inspected.

== Sources ==
<references />
new_people.assessment: William Glasgow-428's 30 September 1746 will directly distinguishes daughter Sarah. Her later life is untraced; the supplied draft preserves her one family role without a mother assignment. The actual Glasgow-2451 and Glasgow-4122 accounts represent Scottish daughters of John, conflicting with Sarah's named father William. Fresh Sarah/Glasgow surname-variant searches found no compatible Glasgow/Glasco/Glascoe historical account. Fuzzy Glass/Glascock and married-surname hits are not accepted on a name score; examined nearby colonial comparisons are recorded in the duplicate audit. Do not conflate Sarah with Lowdenner, Abiah, Elizabeth or the unborn child, or infer her mother from Susanah's status as testator's wife. Father connection reviewed at 99% for this record-defined daughter; the local tree now links her to William Glasgow-428. This adds a missing family edge, not a new reading of the will.

new_people.name: Walter Glasgow of Leithford, buried in 1647
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
Walter Glasgow was indexed as buried on 4 June 1647 in the Kirknewton/East Calder register, with residence Leithford and next of kin William Glasgow, relationship “Son to”. The original is not inspected; burial is not an exact death date.<ref>Findmypast/SGS, Walter Glasgow, burial 4 June 1647, Leithford; OPR 689/20; https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBUR%2F1625437.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The burial precedes both proposed 23 September 1647/1649 baptism dates for Glasgow-1554. It cannot be assigned to that later-born/baptised child on the current chronology. Reuse of the name within one family is possible, but the adult father’s identity and relationship between the two Walters remain unproved.
Inspect OPR 689/20 for the burial and both baptism readings; verify any year heading or transcription error before treating the two Walters as proved siblings or creating a new person.

=== Preferred father and the two Walters — 17 October 2026 ===

[[Glasgow-1087|William Glasgow]] is the selected probable father, at 68% subjective confidence. The transcript’s explicit William father role is assessed at 98%; the same-father Leithford household comparison with the later [[Glasgow-1554|Walter]] is 84%. The 68% identification with the Mid Calder man is a separate, weaker inference; these figures are not independent probabilities. No mother is assigned.

The burial and later baptism name William and the exact Leithford residence, with the same register reference. The later baptism follows the burial under either disputed year, consistent with reuse of a dead child’s name. Another William of Leithford remains the principal alternative; William-3517 and William-1556 lack this local household chain, while the older Leith mealmaker William-3075 is weaker geographically, not excluded solely because he died before the burial.

The two Walters remain separate record accounts pending original-year verification. This source-verification HOLD remains in force; no live creation, merge, exact death date or infant age follows.<ref>Findmypast/SGS, Walter Glasgow burial, 4 June 1647, Leithford, OPR 689/20, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBUR%2F1625437; Walter Glasgow baptism indexed 23 September 1647, same residence/reference, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F4473489. Supplied ScotlandsPeople OPR 690/10/19 and FamilySearch https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-FWL instead give 23 September 1649. William’s Mid Calder christening, 24 December 1609, OPR 694/10/15: https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1B2-3LV. Maintained provider readings reused; originals not inspected in this review.</ref>

The later Walter’s baptism names William at the same Leithford residence and register, supporting one household and reuse of the name after the June 1647 burial. new_people.name: Alexander Elder
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The published headstone transcription for Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church records a memorial erected by Alexander Elder of Gortrickey to his father Robert Elder, his mother Jane, and his sisters and brothers. It also records Alexander Elder's death on 5 January 1943.<ref>Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church headstones; https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/graveyard.html; . This is a new direct memorial transcription for the catalogue's parentage study, not a Glasgow record and not proof that the Elder family was related to Alexander Glasgow. Its value is locality context: Gortrickey/Gortereghy is the townland where the Glasgow family appears in the 1837–1838 Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism entries. The memorial supplies a named Elder household for future comparison with the later Robert Elder who occupied Alexander Glasgow's former Lisnagaver lot; identity between those Elder references remains unproved.</ref>

A 2007 RootsChat research post reproduces a 18 June 1908 Second Portglenone Presbyterian marriage entry for Alexander Elder, full-age bachelor farmer of Gortreaghy, whose father is recorded as Robert Elder, farmer. Alexander married Mary Anderson, full-age spinster of Gortreaghy, daughter of Neil Anderson; witnesses were Robert Anderson and Margaret Elder.<ref>RootsChat, Elder, Murdoch & McMeekin Families; https://www.rootschat.com/forum/index.php?topic=214109.0; . The entry is not yet an inspected original, so it is a secondary-source lead rather than final evidence. It is nevertheless a new, specific parent-bearing record for the Gortreaghy Elder household and gives a testable route for determining whether the Alexander Elder on the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial was a son of the Robert Elder who later occupied Alexander Glasgow's Lisnagaver lot. That identity chain remains unproved.</ref>

The inspected original 1911 Gortereghy census return records Alexander Elder, aged 40, as head, Mary Elder, aged 44, as wife, Robert Elder, aged 34, as brother, and Margaret Elder, aged 25, as sister (Form A, official index house 37, nai001390156, rows 1–4). These stated relationships support comparison with the 1901 household, the 1908 marriage lead and the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial; identification with existing profiles remains qualified.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 Gortereghy return records Robert Elder, 65, widowed farmer, with Alex 27 and Robert 20 as sons and Eliza 22 and Margaretta 14 as daughters. The 1911 Alexander/Mary household explicitly records Robert as Alexander’s brother and Margaret as his sister. The combined names and locality strongly support continuity, with age differences retained. Robert [[Elder-7144]] remains a qualified father identity; Robert/Mary Glasgow’s Gortahar household is separate.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Robert Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298460.pdf; Form A; official index house 42; rows 1–5; 1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Identity revalidation, 17 October 2026: The original 1901 Alex is explicitly Robert’s son; the 1911 return names brother Robert and sister Margaret. Together with the 1908 Alexander/Mary Anderson marriage extract, these support one sibling family. Retain the actual age differences. Use the same qualified Elder-7144 father hypothesis for Alexander and proved siblings; mother Jane on the memorial is separately evidenced, while Jane Calderwood remains a comparison. No matching Alexander profile was established in full same-name and father-filtered searches.

new_people.name: Caroline McCaughern
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The 1911 Gortereghy census browse records Sarah McCaughern, aged 82, as head of household with Matilda Mulholland, 52, and Caroline McCaughern, 47, recorded as daughters; Sara Jane McCaughern, 45, and Jas Alex McCaughern, 43, are also listed as children, with Geo Mulholland, 14, as grandson. It confirms a substantial McCaughern household in the same townland as the Elder and Glasgow-associated records, but it does not identify Sarah's husband, parents or relationship to Mary Glasgow.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 and 1911 returns establish continuity of Sarah McCaughern’s Gortereghy family. Sarah was a Derry-born widow aged 72/82; Caroline, Sarah J/Sara Jane, James A/Jas Alex, Matilda and grandson George occur in both returns. Elizabeth, 32, is also a daughter in 1901. Sarah [[Dysart-1893]], married in 1851 to Gortereghy farmer John McCaughern, remains the strongest mother identity, but neither census names her deceased husband or maiden surname.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298441.pdf; Form A; official index house 18; rows 1–7; 1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6; Rasharkin Presbyterian civil marriage register 1851; https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1851/09402/5405894.pdf; PDF page 1; entry 28. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Identity revalidation, 17 October 2026: Caroline McCaughern/McCarnagh searches returned zero results. McCaughan returned only other given-name or later-generation variants, without a compatible Caroline born about 1864 and daughter of Sarah. No existing profile was identified within this explicit search scope. The original 1901/1911 returns establish the household’s continuity. Carry Dysart-1893 as the qualified mother identity and John McCaughern-23 as the corresponding uncertain father hypothesis for proved siblings. George’s particular mother remains unproved.

new_people.name: Nicholas Glasco / Glascoe
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
Nicholas Glasco is named in a 20 June 1746 report in the ''Weekly Worcester Journal'' among officers in the rebel army committed to New Gaol, Southwark. The notice lists him between John Duncan and Alexander M'Laughlan. It gives no rank for Nicholas individually and does not state a conviction, birthplace, residence, relatives, occupation, or dates of birth or death.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1214317653/ ''Weekly Worcester Journal'', 20 June 1746, p.4], original roster inspected 4 October 2026. Date follows provider metadata; masthead date has not been separately checked.</ref>


The 27 and 28 June reports describe Nicholas Glascoe as a self-styled major and allege a role in the attack on the Hazard sloop. These are allegations, not a finding of guilt.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394536822/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-06-27, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404059808/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-06-28, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

An August report lists Nicholas among persons indicted for high treason, while the 7 November paper announces the pending trial.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404060798/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-08-23, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394542827/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-11-07, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

The 8 and 17 November reports say he was acquitted, with defence evidence identifying him as a French native born at Saint-Germain-en-Laye and a lieutenant in Dillon’s Regiment. They report an order to detain him as a French prisoner. The Caledonian account also mentions a Not Guilty verdict and removal of his bolts; the saved excerpt stops before the full cartel articles. These reports require comparison with the underlying legal and military records.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404061824/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-11-08, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394462695/ The Caledonian Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

In May 1747 a notice names Mr Glascoe as major in Lord Ogilvy’s new regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate, but the missing forename and unproved continuity prevent a firm identification.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404076485/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1747-05-09, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

No parents, spouse, children, birth date, death date or Irish origin is established.

Further original issues preserve June rosters, indictment reprints and Dutch reports, along with acquittal reports containing translated cartel articles. These are related issue appearances; no independent family identity follows. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979338930/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury (The Sherborne Mercury, or Weekly Advertiser), 1746-06-30, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334222061/ S Gravenhaegse Courant, 1746-09-21, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979339079/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971385255/ The Gloucester Journal, 1746-11-18, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334158733/ Opregte Haarlemsche Courant, 1746-12-01, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

The Gloucester Journal of 28 April 1747 describes Major Glascoe as lately discharged at London and chief major in Lord Ogilvy’s projected regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate; no forename is given, and English pay is not interpreted as British military service.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971516263/ Gloucester Journal, 28 April 1747, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The rare full name, Southwark proceedings and Hazard episode support a probable association across the 1746 reports. French birth and service are reported defence evidence. They do not establish an Irish origin, a Glasgow-family connection or relatives. The May 1747 appointment lacks a forename.

new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''Bessie Glasgow''' lived at Quodquen, now Quothquan in Lanarkshire, in 1650. She was the lawful sister of [[Glasgow-3296|John Glasgow]], whose testament dative and inventory were confirmed at Lanark on 27 May 1650. The opening calls Bessie his lawful sister; the confirmation calls the deceased John her brother and identifies her as his executrix dative.<ref name="Quothquan1650">National Records of Scotland, Lanark Commissary Court, testament dative and inventory of John Glasgow in Quodquen, confirmed 27 May 1650, CC14/5/5, register images 65–66; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills Scotland's People wills search]. The sibling clauses and continuity of both images were visually checked in the maintained original-image review of 10 September 2026; the full opening and accounts are not yet completely transcribed.</ref><ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., ''The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800'' (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1903), printed p. 38, “Glasgow, John, in Quodquen,” 27 May 1650, [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments__1595-1800_~_1903.pdf#page=50 digital copy, PDF p. 50]. The calendar confirms John's estate entry; the original supplies Bessie's relationship.</ref>

Bessie was alive at that confirmation and was born before 1650. No age, birthplace, death date, spouse or child has been established. Quothquan is her recorded residence, not an established birthplace or death place.<ref name="Quothquan1650" />

== Research Notes ==
=== Family and identity ===
The two sibling clauses support the record-defined John–Bessie relationship at '''99% subjective confidence'''; they belong to one testament, not two independent sources. Bessie's identity among existing profiles remains unresolved. Compatible candidates include [[Glasgow-3361|Bessie Glasgow of South Leith, indexed in 1616]], [[Glasgow-1091|Elizabeth Glasgow of Glasgow, baptised in 1616]], [[Glasgow-1092|Bessie Glasgow of Glasgow, indexed in 1623]] and [[Glasgow-1517|Elizabeth Glasgow of Glasgow, christened in 1625]]. No baptism or later household is assigned to this woman merely from the shared name.

[[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]] is the selected uncertain father of Bessie's brother John, assessed at '''22% subjective probability'''. Extending that same paternal hypothesis to the documented sister gives Bessie a '''conditional 22%''' placement. Stephen's adult Glasgow life in 1575 and marriage to [[Graham-38221|Margaret Grahame]] in 1582 permit the proposed generation, but do not connect that household to the Quothquan siblings.<ref>Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. 7, protocol 2189, printed p. 110, 17 June 1575, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc00robegoog/page/n126/mode/2up digital copy]; vol. 8, protocol 2431, 25 June 1582, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto08glas/page/56/mode/2up digital copy]. These name Stephen's parents and spouse, respectively, not Bessie or the Quothquan John as his children.</ref> This placement is dependent on John's hypothesis and adds no independent evidence for Stephen's paternity. Bessie's mother remains unknown; Margaret Grahame is not thereby her mother. No candidate baptism profile's documented parentage is changed by this conditional model.

Bessie Glasgow must be distinguished from [[Robertson-33965|Bessie Robertson]], the deceased spouse of a John Glasgow in Montfoid whose testament was confirmed in 1610.<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., ''The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800'' (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1901), [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/n435/mode/1up p. 426], Robertson, Bessie, 17 August 1610; cross-reference under Glasgow, John, [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/196/mode/1up p. 196].</ref> The Montfoid husband's identity with the Quothquan deceased is itself uncertain.
